scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Footwork music first appeared in the late 1990s to early 2000s as a faster and increasingly abstract variant of ghetto house, evolving to match the energy of footwork dance born in Chicago ghettos and underground dance competitions.
Pioneers like RP Boo, DJ Rashad, and DJ Clent developed the sound, notably when DJs started playing ghetto house records at 45 RPM instead of 33 RPM.
Crew formations like 'Beatdown House' and 'House-O-Matics' anchored its early development.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Footwork functions as a high-energy outlet for spontaneous expression and competitive challenge.

It serves as a vital component of club culture and urban youth expression, providing a structured yet abstract framework for physical improvisation and community connection across Chicago and international hubs.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is a style of street dance closely associated with juke and footwork music, typified by very fast and chaotic feet moves.
It involves rapid movements of the legs, arms, and body accompanied by twists and turns.
Performances and practice sessions regularly take place in the form of a 'battle' where dancers face off and improvise.
Watch for Fast footwork.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Footwork songs are generally around 150–165 BPM with beat-skipping kick drums pounding rapidly in syncopation with crackling snares, claps, and drum machine elements like the Roland TR-808, often produced using an MPC.
Tracks feature heavily syncopated samples from rap, pop, R&B, and soul, which may be up- or down-pitched.
Listen for the Roland TR-808, MPC.
The pulse is Syncopated / Ternary feel at about 157 beats a minute.
A hyper-rhythmic, fast-paced electronic music around 160 BPM featuring beat-skipping kick drums, syncopated claps, heavy sub-bass lines, and chopped vocal samples.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Footwork is set in underground dance competitions, house parties, club venues, and community spaces such as the Underground Tracks Factory in Chicago, as well as international clubs in cities like London, Paris, and Osaka.
Dancers typically wear casual streetwear suitable for high-speed, athletic movement.

Reconstruction imagery allowed only from the costume notes, labelled 'reconstruction'

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures in the footwork movement include RP Boo (credited with founding tracks like 'Baby Come On'), DJ Rashad (leader of Teklife and producer of Double Cup), DJ Clent, DJ Spinn, DJ Diamond, DJ Roc, DJ Nate, and international proponents such as DJ Fulltono in Japan and Tiger Heslop in London.

Regional variants include proper juke music (which relies on a four-to-the-floor house rhythm rather than abstract beat-skipping), Juketon (combining juke with reggaeton, pioneered by DJ Chi-C in Chicago and Mexico), Party-Juke in Japan (incorporating rap vocals and otaku culture), and European adaptations in cities like London and Paris.
Footwork descends directly from ghetto house and house dance, while incorporating elements of hip-hop, drum & bass, and jungle.
